newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Britain's Rifkind gives Romania new NATO chances.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rifkind gives Romania new NATO chances.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Tuesday that Romania's new commitment to reform and improved relations with Hungary and Ukraine had boosted its chances of quick admission to NATO.

Rifkind told a news conference after talks with newly elected President Emil Constantinescu that members of the Atlantic alliance had been impressed by the centrist government since it ousted ex-communists in November elections.
"For Britain as for other NATO countries the events of the last few months have been important. They have demonstrated the strength of Romania's democratic institutions," Rifkind said.

"They have revived the commitment to genuine market economic reforms. And they have shown further improvements in the relationship between Romania and its neighbours. These have certainly helped Romania's case with regard to NATO."
Rifkind, the most senior Western official to visit Romania since Constantinescu's victory ended the seven-year rule of ex-communists, travelled on to Bulgaria later in the day.

Romania has pushed hard for inclusion in the first wave of NATO expansion, due to be announced at the alliance's July summit in Madrid. But it has so far been seen as an outsider behind favourites Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
Romanian Foreign Minister Andrei Severin told reporters he hoped NATO would "finally recognise the principle of a simultaneous admission of all countries belonging to the same geo-strategic region".

Romania's main backer has been France, which last week assured the Bucharest leadership it would support its bid. French President Jacques Chirac is expected to reinforce that support when he visits Bucharest next month.
Constantinescu has pledged to speed market reforms and talks are under way with the International Monetary Fund. Top level visits have already taken place to Poland and Hungary.

Rifkind singled out for praise Romania's conclusion last September of a treaty with Hungary, ironing out longstanding disputes over borders and minority rights, and Bucharest's efforts to clinch a similar agreement with Ukraine.
"I pay tribute to the very good progress in the historic relationship between Romania and Hungary and the priority given to the relationship between Romania and Ukraine," he said.
Even if Romania was included among first-wave admissions, he said, the alliance faced the challenge of ensuring good relations with other countries which did not seek membership.
That principally meant Russia, which opposes NATO expansion, and Ukraine, which is not seeking membership but has no objection to the alliance's move eastward.
"Enlargement must not take place in isolation, it must be accompanied by the achievement of a good healthy stragetic relationship between NATO and Russia," Rifkind said.

"It must also be accompanied by the development of a good healthy relationship between NATO and those European countries that may not wish to join NATO but have common interests in European security of which the most important is Ukraine."

Romanian officials recognise that improved relations with Ukraine are vital for their NATO membership bid. Bucharest also wants to mend fences with Moscow after seven years of cool relations since the fall of communism.

Talks with Ukraine resumed this month with both sides trying to overcome the main snag -- Bucharest's insistence that Kiev atone for the loss of Romanian lands to Moscow under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact. Similar treaties remain unsigned with Russia and ex-Soviet Moldova, mainly for the same reasons.
